articles.title: Sony and Nintendo Should Keep the Current Gen Going for as Long as Possible 'Because People Are Very Happy Using PS5 and Switch 2,' Former PlayStation Exec Says
articles.summary: Sony and Nintendo need to make their current consoles last as long as possible amid soaring costs, former PlayStation exec Shuhei Yoshida has said.
articles.body:
Sony and Nintendo need to make their current consoles last as long as possible amid soaring costs that have already prompted PS5 and Switch 2 price rises.

That's according to former PlayStation Worldwide Studios boss Shuhei Yoshida, who told The Verge that console companies needed to focus on sustaining their current hardware platforms for "as long as possible."

While there's no suggestion that Nintendo plans to launch a Switch 3 anytime soon (Switch 2 only arrived last year!), the company always devotes a chunk of its budget to researching future hardware. And upgrades to the launch Switch 2 model will undoubtedly be considered at some point, similar to the Switch Lite and Switch OLED.

As for Sony, we know that a PlayStation 6 is on the way at some point . Previously, analysts had suggested a 2028 launch seemed likely, though Sony is yet to make any official indication of when PS6 may arrive — and as time goes on, that late 2028 release date feels less and less likely . Indeed, Yoshida has suggested that console makers may now be looking to delay the arrival of next-gen hardware as long as possible.

"Sony and Nintendo have sold enough numbers of their current-generation hardware, so because of the cost of goods, they might be looking [at] pushing back the launch of next gen," Yoshida said. "I think they should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2.

"People have [a] finite budget, and it feels like PC and consoles, the components very specific to these devices have increased their price way more than all the other forms of entertainment," he continued. "People who have systems like PS5, Switch 2, or PCs – you know, good enough PCs – probably will be happy to play games on them and not necessarily consider replacing [them]."

The key issue here is the skyrocketing cost of computer memory, AKA "RAMageddon", fuelled in part by the rise of AI datacenters. In short, memory production resources are limited, and much of next year's production output is already spoken for. Should Sony, for example, want to start manufacturing a new console anytime soon, it may be physically unable to do so in the volume it would like — let alone being able to sell the console for a price that consumers would pay.

As a reminder, the Sony launched its PS5 with a disc drive for $500, while its digital-only counterpart sold for $400. These machines now cost $650 and $600 respectively — price rises of $150 and $200 since 2020. PS5 Pro launched at $700, meanwhile, and now costs $900. It's hard to see PS6 arriving at much less than $1,000. Switch 2, meanwhile, has risen in price by $50 since launch last year, from $450 to $500.

And then there's the general lack of desire from both consumers or developers for machines capable of drastically better performance, something Yoshida also noted. The only exception to this is Xbox, which has been more vocal about its push towards a next-gen offering with Project Helix . The difference with Microsoft's team, though, is it has not sold truckloads of consoles of late.

"I don't think lots of people are asking for more power — 'We need more power!' — or even developers," Yoshida concluded. "I don't think developers are asking [for] better hardware! So I think that means that the current generation, Sony and Nintendo are going to do pretty well for many years to come, still.

"Xbox is a team who wants to change the competing landscape, so it's going to be hard for them, but it's their time to play. It's very exciting, what's going to happen next year?"

articles.title: Tom Cruise Is Back in Digger, a Film About Environmental Catastrophe That the Fossil Fools Running Things Are Too Ill-Equipped to Solve
articles.summary: Review: Digger's satire may not change your thinking on global warming, but there are excellent performances from Tom Cruise and the rest of the cast, and more than a few laughs.
articles.body:
"Gentlemen, we find ourselves in a dildo of a pickle," says the President of the United States as he comes to grips with the fact that a US oil-drilling mishap has split off a city-sized ice shelf that's on a path of destruction toward Europe and will trigger tsunamis, causing untold death and destruction. That line, exquisitely delivered by John Goodman and imposingly photographed by director Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Babel, Birdman, The Revenant) in his signature low, wide-angle style, also sums up my complex feelings toward a film whose reach far exceeds its grasp and whose satire—while funny—would have felt fresher a decade ago.

Starting with an ice fracture "10 times the size of his own dick," Digger follows Digger Rockwell, the oil tycoon responsible for the ice shelf debacle mentioned above, who finds himself on the defensive as he works with the president, advisors and generals to try to stop the impending doom brought on by our insatiable appetite for fossil fuels—and when that fails, at the very least, to "control the narrative."

There's a twist that the marketing seems to be deliberately trying to avoid, so I won't directly mention it in this review. However, it fundamentally affects my opinion of the film. I'll talk around it and also fence it in with "Possible Spoiler" warnings.

But let's get right to the best part of the show: Tom Cruise.

It's been a long time since Tom Cruise has taken on a role that required zero action. I was excited for him to enter his post-Mission: Impossible era and was delighted to see elements of Digger Rockwell echo Tropic Thunder's Les Grossman.

For Digger Rockwell, Cruise dons heavy prosthetics to fully transform into the wily old oil tycoon. His look may be more Ross Perot, but it’s still clear an action star is under all that latex, climbing mantles and dancing with his shovel. Whether he's bickering with Riz Ahmed about his annoying scientific ethics or lecturing world leaders on why he's necessary—the latter of which is one of the best scenes in the film and might be worth the price of admission alone—Cruise's performance is both focused and kinetic.

Digger lecturing a United Nations-type body is Cruise's "you can't handle the truth!" monologue and might be one of the best of his career. His "You demand. I supply" rhetoric echoes Colonel Jessup's "[you] sleep under the blanket of the very freedom I provide, and then you question the manner in which I provide it" speech. Instead of Nicholson's fierce but measured delivery (which Nerdwriter expertly broke down in his Jack Nicholson: The Art of Anger video essay), Digger delivers this whole speech while pacing the set and even physically fighting with some listeners in one unbroken take.

For every Tom Cruise action movie, there's some featurette of the filmmakers marveling at his ability to deliver a line while he's dangling from a building or strapped to the side of a plane. Digger's monologue, where he conjures up an almost 1,000-word lecture without cutting, all while hitting the constantly moving camera blocking, is as stunning an accomplishment and as mesmerizing as any of those action scenes.

This scene isn't just Tom at his best; it's also Iñárritu and longtime collaborator, cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, upping their game too. This Digger oner combines the complex blocking of background and extras from Birdman's Times Square underwear jaunt with the more dialogue-heavy long shots Iñárritu and Lubezki experimented with in The Revenant to create a stunning one-shot that showcases Cruise's acting chops in a way we haven't seen in decades, if ever.

Thematically, this monologue is one of the few times the satire actually says something pointed. Most of the film relies on a Looney Tunes-esque, Yosemite Sam diplomacy: We need oil at any cost and American weapons and brute force can solve any problem nature presents.

Digger's speech provides a smart contrast to the President's mean-spirited, selfish, extremely aggressive, and idiotic decisions. His monologue deftly navigates a complex and evolving argument that starts with that "You demand, I supply" line before chastising the attendees for profiting royally from his companies, explaining that the masses are too poor to care, and finally lecturing them that they've inadvertently chosen his side in these matters, so they better pray he wins.

Digger represents the status quo, personified. Iñárritu uses this monologue as the film's sharpest argument for how Digger and company's poor decision-making got them into an environmental catastrophe that these fossil fools are too ill-equipped to solve.

This is a film about how methane leaks caused by the prolonged burning of fossil fuels, combined with an oil-drilling fiasco, created an environmental catastrophe that the film's clearly conservative leadership is ill-equipped to deal with. To avoid bringing politics into this review is a diplomatic exercise that only John Goodman's president would be stupid enough to pursue.

Political satire doesn't need to be subtle, but it does need to illuminate something beyond the obvious by pushing story elements like recognizable characters, plots, and events to their logical extremes. Unfortunately, the script by Iñárritu, Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone, and Sabina Berman fails to provoke any profound truth or unique thinking. The end of this global-warming disaster satire lands exactly where you think it will. Regrettably for Digger, there are other films like Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up that have tackled the same topics, but in more interesting ways.

There’s been a lot of reporting on the mixed early impressions of Digger. Don't Look Up’s reaction was also mixed. It currently has a 56% on Rotten Tomatoes. But IGN gave it a 7/10, and I more or less agree with our review. McKay's different, and in my opinion, smarter approach to the topic—using an asteroid impact as a metaphor for global warming—created a more nuanced take on the subject. He used an objectively obvious catastrophe to contrast our society's inability to do anything to stop it because of our culture's unholy mix of greed, politics, and misinformation.

Digger does the exact opposite of Don't Look Up: Instead of indecision, things go worse because the film's leaders make profoundly stupid decisions. Digger still made me laugh at a decent amount of the jokes, but the film will probably alienate a large part of the audience due to the cartoonishly selfish and negligent conservative politicians and businessmen—characters like Goodman's President Compson and his cabinet, who embody the most negative stereotypes of the American right wing. Meanwhile, some on the other side might bristle at rampant machismo and misogyny that are done in the name of satire.

There's a twist in Digger. I'm going to talk around it here.

A big theme in Digger is "controlling the narrative," which Digger believes is crucial to maintaining power. To that end, we need to talk about Jesse Plemons' character.

I've lamented how unrefined the film's characters are. Only twice does its blunt satire say something interesting: the first is Digger's monologue, and the second is a speech from Plemons' character.

When I left the theater, it was Plemons' monologue that kept me thinking about the film. Without getting too deep into spoilers, his monologue touches on themes explored in the 2022 documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed, a film about how the Sackler family used its money to fund the arts to rehabilitate its image after its role in America's opioid crisis. Plemons' character smartly touches on these same ideas, putting an interesting spin on Digger's story in the final act.

There's an old filmmaking adage: "You can make a bad movie from a good script, but you can't make a good movie from a bad script." Unfortunately, the script is Digger's Achilles heel. But that doesn't mean there isn't some exceptional work on display.

From frame one, it's completely obvious that this movie looks expensive. From evocative murals to stylized miniature work to window vistas that look like amazing natural history museum dioramas, production designer Dennis Gassner created a world that is overflowing with detail and style worthy of a Wes Anderson movie.

Riz Ahmed, who plays Ganesh, Digger's lead scientist and the voice of reason, spars frequently with Tom Cruise, making for some of the film's best exchanges. This probably won't be the movie that lands Cruise his acting statue, but Ahmed turns in the kind of generous supporting performance that Cruise was known for in the late '80s and early '90s which helped his co-stars land Academy Awards.

John Goodman also delivers a stellar performance as President Compson. He has some of the best lines, and you can tell he had a hell of a time delivering them on set.

articles.title: Xbox’s Mythic Achievements are here and they’re just like PlayStation Platinum trophies
articles.summary: Xbox testers can try out the new Mythic Achievements today.
articles.body: Microsoft is officially announcing its new Xbox Mythic Achievements today, and they’re already available for Xbox Insiders to test. Mythic Achievements work a lot like Sony’s PlayStation Platinum trophies and are unlocked once you’ve earned every original achievement for a game. “Mythic Achievements have already been added to eligible games you completed in the past, including Xbox 360 titles,” says the Xbox team. “The next time you visit your profile, you may discover that some of your favorite games have already reached Mythic status.” [Image: You’ll be able to track Mythic Achievements easily from the Xbox dashboard. Xbox profiles will soon include a new gaming tab that lets you track Gamerscore milestones and Mythic Achievements. The main Achievements list is also being updated to make it easier to track Mythic status. “A new progress bar at the top of each game’s achievement list shows how close you are to Mythic status, with an option to focus on the original achievements you still need,” says team Xbox. Mythic Achievements leaked as part of an Xbox PC app last week, complete with a unique unlock sound. Mythic Achievements are now in testing just weeks after Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed that Xbox would be getting a platinum trophy equivalent later this year.

articles.title: GTA 6 Reveal Crashes Game Informer App Amid Confusion Over Free Coverage
articles.summary: Game Informer's website and app crashed today amid the debut of its exclusive GTA 6 preview, creating chaos among fans.
articles.body:
Game Informer's website and app crashed today amid the debut of its exclusive GTA 6 preview, creating chaos among fans.

Game Informer has released a 14-page cover story with all kinds of new information on GTA 6 today, but unfortunately fans are struggling to access it. The second the story went live, Game Informer's website crashed. Just prior to the release of the coverage, it was confirmed that the story would be made free to all users through Game Informer's app. As you might imagine, this led to the site being overwhelmed with traffic.
